common_name: Twin Sisters Daffodil (Butter and Eggs Tazetta)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Twin Sisters is an ancient sterile tazetta hybrid spread entirely by bulb division and has been passed hand to hand between Gulf South gardeners for well over a century, naturalizing at old homesites, cemeteries, and roadsides.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Twin Sisters gets its common name from its habit of producing exactly two fragrant flowers per stem, each with pure white perianth segments surrounding a small, pale yellow cup, blooming earlier than most trumpet daffodils in mid to late winter. It is an ancient sterile hybrid that sets no seed, so like Grand Primo and Grand Monarque it has survived and spread across the Deep South for generations purely as a pass-along bulb, still turning up blooming reliably each year at abandoned homesites long after everything else planted there is gone. Give it a low-chill spot in full sun, let the foliage die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply for years.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bulbs for Texas

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to fall, setting the rhizome shallow with its top just at or barely below the soil surface in well-drained soil in full sun; Cemetery Iris is a sterile, ancient bearded iris spread entirely by hand-me-down rhizome division, which is exactly how it reached the countless Southern graveyards and homesites where it still blooms every spring with no care at all.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Cemetery Iris earns its common name from its long association with old Southern graveyards, where it was traditionally planted at gravesites for its clean white, faintly fragrant blooms and because, once established, it needs no attention whatsoever and will outlive the person who planted it by generations. It is an ancient, sterile bearded iris hybrid believed to have spread out of the Mediterranean along old trade and pilgrimage routes centuries ago, reproducing only by rhizome offsets, so every planting traces back to a division from an older clump. It blooms for a few weeks in mid-spring on sturdy stems above gray-green fans of foliage, tolerates poor, dry soil far better than modern bearded iris hybrids, and is essentially immune to the fungal rot that plagues iris grown in humid, poorly drained ground.

common_name: Sweet Iris (Orris Root Iris, Dalmatian Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to fall, setting the rhizome shallow with its top exposed to the sun in well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Iris is an old dooryard-garden heirloom passed along by division for centuries and is the historic source of orris root, the dried, violet-scented rhizome once widely used in perfumery.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallow, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Iris is an old Mediterranean bearded iris long grown in Southern dooryard gardens and passed hand to hand as a heirloom pass-along plant. It bears fragrant, soft lavender-blue flowers with a sweet, grape-like scent in mid-spring above handsome silvery gray-green foliage that stays attractive through summer even after bloom finishes. Historically, its dried, aged rhizome was the primary commercial source of orris root, prized in perfumery and sachets for a violet-like fragrance that develops only after long curing, though modern gardeners grow it mainly for its flowers and foliage. Like other bearded irises, it resents wet feet and rich, heavy soil — give it excellent drainage and avoid mulch piled against the rhizome to prevent rot.

planting.note: Plant divisions (fans) in spring or fall in full sun to partial shade in almost any well-drained soil; Kwanso is the classic double-flowered sport of the orange ditch daylily and, like the species, spreads by stolons and is completely sterile, so it survives and spreads only by hand division and pass-along sharing.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in almost any well-drained soil; Kwanso is a centuries-old double-flowered sport of the orange ditch daylily, producing ruffled, tawny-orange blooms with extra petals crowded into the center of each flower instead of the species' simple six-petaled form. Like its parent, each flower lasts only a single day but the clump produces a long, heavy succession of bloom over three to four weeks in early summer, and the plant is triploid and essentially sterile, spreading only vegetatively by stolons and thick, fleshy roots. It shares the species' legendary toughness, shrugging off clay, drought, heat, and root competition from nearby trees, and has been passed along between Southern gardeners for generations as an easy, reliable heirloom. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigorous bloom and to share starts with other gardeners, exactly as it has spread for centuries.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Naples Onion is an old pass-along bulb of the Deep South, naturalizing readily at abandoned homesites and persisting for decades with no care once established.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Naples Onion is a Mediterranean flowering allium long naturalized as a Southern pass-along bulb, sending up loose, airy umbels of fragrant, star-shaped white flowers on slender stems in early to mid spring, ahead of most other spring bulbs. It multiplies steadily by offset bulbs and, in mild climates, by self-seeding, gradually forming dense colonies in lawns, old flower borders, and untended corners of abandoned homesites where it has quietly persisted for generations. Foliage emerges in fall and should be left to die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulbs for next year; once established, clumps need no supplemental water or feeding to keep returning and spreading each spring.
